## Results

Framework for investigating IDR motifs essential for PS
To facilitate the investigation of PS IDRs and motifs within, we proposed a framework that utilizes computational predictions for hypothesis formulation and PS experiments for hypothesis validation (Fig. 1a). Specifically, for an IDR of interest, the PS propensity is predicted based on its sequence. For high PS propensity IDR, reverse inference provides the relative importance of each region and thus predicts key regions or motifs. The motifs can be validated through mutation experiments, in which the disruption of motifs would attenuate or even eliminate PS of IDRs while the negative control resulted in insignificant effects. The motifs are clustered according to their compositional features, which represent the underlying principles. If the attenuation of PS is rescued by substituting mutated motifs with generated motifs with similar features, the validity of motif features would be confirmed. Through the prediction, generation and validation framework, researchers would be able to capture the molecular determinants of PS IDRs.

Establishment of sequence-based high PS propensity IDR deep learning model
We organized the dataset by leveraging both IDRs prediction and PS propensity predictions. Comprehensive proteome-wide IDRs were identified using several predictors and the consecutive residues were kept. We used PhaSePred, a comprehensive multimodal PS protein predictor, to predict the PS propensities of these IDR-containing proteins11. Based on the predictions, we established our dataset: IDRs from proteins with high predicted PS propensity were denoted as positive set (“high propensity” set), while IDRs from proteins with low predicted propensity were used as negative set (“background propensity” set) (Supplementary Fig. 1a). We selected an optimal threshold for positive set IDRs in order to balance the true positive rate and precision, minimizing potential noise from predicted labels (Supplementary Fig. 1b) (Methods). As a result, a total of 3,131 IDRs with high PS propensity and 11,763 IDRs with background propensity in human proteome were collected (Supplementary Data 1). This dataset was randomly split into training, validation, and test subsets (3:1:1), which were confirmed to be balanced, diverse, and compositionally similar (Supplementary Fig. 1c-f). A similar approach was conducted to collect datasets in other species, which were used for model validation afterwards (Supplementary Fig. 1g).

Explaining the internal behavior of deep learning models has been extensively studied and attention mechanism are dominating the explainability of deep models26. We presumed that by predicting the PS propensity of an IDR using attention-based models, the relative importance of each region within the input sequence is determined. The most important regions identified in this way can represent potential motifs essential for PS to some extent. Hence, we built PhaSeMotif, an interpretable attention-based deep learning model for high PS propensity IDR prediction. Due to the variability in IDR lengths, the model accepts IDR sequences of arbitrary length to enhance ease of use. The input sequences are processed using one-hot encoding based on the amino acids and the amino acid alphabet (Supplementary Table 1, Methods). The model consists primarily of convolutional layers27, multi-head attention layer24, pyramid pooling layers, fully connected layers, and an output layer (Fig. 1b). The convolutional layers are responsible for extracting local features (15 residues in this context), while the attention mechanism layers capture both regional and global relationships within the sequence. The pyramid pooling layers convert inputs of arbitrary length into fixed-length representations, facilitating subsequent fully connected layers for output probability28. The model was trained with training and validation set and the performance was then evaluated with the independent test set (Methods). The final area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of PhaSeMotif in test set achieved 0.86 (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 1h) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) achieved 0.69 (Supplementary Fig. 1i), demonstrating its strong performance. PhaSeMotif also displayed similar performance in datasets of other four species (Fig. 1c). The distribution of PhaSeMotif prediction scores between validation and test datasets were similar and around 30% of human IDRs were scored above 0.5 (Supplementary Fig. 1j).

Due to the scarcity of experimentally verified short specific regions that are essential for PS, we compared the performance of PhaSeMotif with other methods in identifying high PS propensity IDRs. PhaSeMotif achieved the highest AUROC of 0.86 compared to 0.76-0.80 for other methods (Fig. 1d), and the highest AUPRC of 0.69 compared to 0.48-0.60 for other methods (Fig. 1e). To reduce potential bias from full-length sequence predictions, we also selected proteins with IDR fractions of no less than 80% as an additional test set (Supplementary Data 1). PhaSeMotif consistently outperformed other methods in these comparisons with the highest AUROC of 0.96 versus 0.85-0.92 for others and the highest AUPRC of 0.90 versus 0.69-0.81 for others (Supplementary Fig. 1k-l), demonstrating its strong performance.

Multiple IDRs of the same protein may contribute differently to PS behavior. Even though we assigned the same PS labels for all IDRs within the same protein, we found that the predicted probabilities reflect the actual PS capability differences. hnRNPDL, an RNA binding protein, bears arginine-rich and tyrosine-rich IDRs at the N- and C-terminus. The C-terminus IDR underwent PS, possibly through pi-pi interactions, and had a stronger self-aggregation tendency. In contrast, the N-terminus IDR could not undergo PS itself29. In PhaSeMotif prediction, the PS score of C terminus IDR is 0.97 while that of N terminus IDR is 0.33, reflecting real-world difference (Supplementary Fig. 1m). Similarly, the N terminus IDR of ARID1A was predicted as PS IDR (score 0.99), consistent with a previous report that the N terminus PLD underwent PS30. While the other IDR closer to C terminus was predicted less likely to be PS IDR (score 0.38) (Supplementary Fig. 1m).

PhaSeMotif extracted IDR motifs using guided backpropagation and attention scores
As mentioned above, convolution and attention layers captured regional and global features during training. We utilized guided backpropagation (GBP), a gradient-based method to interpret deep learning models25, and attention scores24 to extract the attribution of input IDR’s motifs that lead to the final positive prediction. Specifically, during GBP, only activated neurons with positive forward and backward gradients were retained (denoted as positive regions) (Supplementary Fig. 2a). As each positive region was the weighted combination of the input regions, larger attention scores reflect more important original input regions. Subsequently, we determined a cut-off to identify the lists of most important input regions and defined the attribution score of each input region as the relative frequency that it had been included in the positive regions set (Fig. 2a). Notably, as longer IDR sequence often harbors more IDR motifs, the cut off setting was relevant to the length of individual IDR (Methods). Consequently, the regions with top attribution scores were retained and merged, resulting in the final determination of motifs. Overall, we identified a total of 17594 motifs derived from 2418 PS IDRs through this approach (Supplementary Data 2). More than 59% of motifs were shorter than 20 amino acids (Fig. 2b), which represent a small fraction of IDRs (Fig. 2b).

Take the C terminus IDR of hnRNPDL as an example, 4 important regions were identified and merged into 2 motifs (Fig. 2d). Previous research highlighted the importance of tyrosine residues in mediating homotypic pi-pi interactions within IDRs and heterotypic cation-pi interactions with positive charged residues8,29. Here we found that tyrosine residues were enriched in these two motifs, consistent with previous findings. The other example is G3BP1, which modulates stress granule assembly31,32. PhaSeMotif predicted that its largest PS motif resided near C terminus while its N terminus was less important (Fig. 2e). Indeed, the C terminus RG-rich are crucial for PS and the acidic region near N terminus negatively regulate PS, which is highly aligned with PhaSeMotif prediction. In the case of G3BP1, relative importance also reflects the ability of attention-based mechanism to capture the global relationships between regions. Ubiquilin-2 (UBQLN2), a protein involved in protein degradation, forms stress-induced biomolecular condensates. Proline-rich region and ST1-II domain (UBQLN2379-624) are necessary for UBQLN2 PS and where most amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) related mutations reside33,34. The PhaSeMotif identified motifs were in line with these important regions (Fig. 2f). hnRNPA1 is known as a Prion-like domain (PLD) containing protein20, whose PS behavior is determined largely by the aromatic residues. PhaSeMotif identifies three motifs within the important PLD, each containing several aromatic residues (Fig. 2g). TIA1 is an RNA-binding protein and a component of stress granule. PhaSeMotif predicts two motifs which TIA1 C-terminal IDR, which contains proline residues for regulating its PS35 (Fig. 2h). NPM1 is abundant in the nucleolus and undergoes PS through electrostatic interactions. Within the NPM1 IDR enriched with charged residues, PhaSeMotif identifies one motif within the basic residue-enriched tract that mediates homotypic interactions and PS36,37 (Fig. 2i).

As PhaSeMotif provides finer-grained measurements of relative importance within IDRs, we examined whether the motifs recognized mutations that affect PS. We extracted point mutations from PhaSepDB and evaluated their effects of mutations on PS based on the original literature (Supplementary Data 3). The mutations were classified into two categories: those that severely eliminate PS (major effect mutations) and those with only a slight influence (minor effect mutations). For example, UBQLN2 P506T significantly impaired PS and condensate formation, while mutants such as A282V, M446R only showed little difference compared to wild type (WT)34. By comparing the mutation sites to predicted motifs by PhaSeMotif (Supplementary Fig. 2b), we found that major effect mutations are more likely to be located within motifs compared to minor effect mutations. Specifically, 12 out of 21 (57%) major effect mutations are covered by PS motifs, compared to only 21% (9/43) of minor effect mutations. When considering only self-assembly PS proteins, 11 out of 17 (65%) mutations fall within motifs (Fig. 2j). We normalized the PhaSeMotif attribution scores as z-scores across the IDRs and compared the distribution of major effect mutation sites to background controls (Supplementary Fig. 2c). The results show that major effect mutations have significantly higher scores than background controls (Fig. 2k). Overall, these results demonstrate that while PhaSeMotif may not capture all mutations related to PS, it is effective at identifying motifs that contain mutations with major effects on PS.

The accuracy and specificity of PhaSeMotif predictions were experimentally validated
In order to further validate the effectiveness of PhaSeMotif, we performed in-cell PS experiments with wild type (WT) and motif mutated IDRs (Mut) (Fig. 3a). The optogenetic optoDroplets system were constructed as previously described38,39. Specifically, the IDR was fused to the fluorescent protein mCherry and the blue light-sensitive protein Cry2, which form Cry2 oligomers and induce the formation of IDR droplets under blue light stimulation (Methods). First, we have selected 12 IDRs from top-ranking PS IDRs predicted by PhaSeMotif, derived from proteins namely hnRNPH1, CPEB2, TAF15, MLLT1, TIA1, TDP43, FMR1, EP300, FUS, and DDX4. More than 90% of these IDRs are scored above 0.90, while 33% of them are over 0.99 (Supplementary Data 4). Upon blue light inducement, all of the IDRs displayed fast droplet formation in cells within 1–2 min, which indicated successful construction of optoDroplets and the PS capability of selected IDRs (Fig. 3b–m, Supplementary Fig. 3b–d). The progression of droplet formation was assessed semi-quantitatively through the number of fluorescent puncta in cells over time.

PhaSeMotif identified motifs with high attribution scores, and we speculated that disrupting these regions would lead to the attenuated PS of IDRs (Fig. 3a). Hence, we engineered motifs within IDRs by replacing them with (GGS)n, a flexible and hydrophilic linker, maintaining the original length40. This modification resulted in a total of 17 distinct mutated IDRs (Supplementary Fig. 3e, Supplementary Data 4). The PS propensities of motif-mutated IDRs were examined in the same approach. As a result, the droplet formation was significantly attenuated in 82% (14/17) mutated IDRs. The condensate formation was almost eliminated in CPEB2, TDP43, TIA1, EP300, hnRNPH1, TAF15, FMR1 and MLLT1 Mut1/2/4 IDRs compared to corresponding WT (Fig. 3b–m), except for DDX4, ASCL1 and FUS IDRs (Supplementary Fig. 3b–d). The formation rate and intracellular puncta number of MLLT1 Mut3 largely decreased (Fig. 3i). Considering the relatively small length of mutated motifs (Fig. 2c), it’s likely that the affected PS activities were due to disruption of important interactions rather than overall sequence change. Besides, most of the tested motifs expand current knowledge and do not overlap with known mutations that weaken PS in PhaSepDB. (Supplementary Data 4). Together, these results highlight PhaSeMotif’s potential to identify important sequence motifs related to PS.

Meanwhile, we investigated the specificity of PhaSeMotif’s predictions. While several existing PS protein prediction methods provide residue-level scores, their putatively important regions often span a large fraction. To demonstrate the enhanced specificity of PhaSeMotif, we conducted negative control (NC) experiments in addition to the positive predictions. In these NC experiments, regions outside the predicted motifs of PhaSeMotif were substituted with (GGS)n repeats. The NC1/2/3 regions of TDP43 are located within the important regions predicted by catGRANULE, PLAAC and FuzDrop (Fig. 3d), while the NC1/2 regions of CPEB2 (Fig. 3b) and NC1 region of TIA1 (Fig. 3f) are located within important regions predicted by PLAAC and FuzDrop. Compared with WT IDR, the NC mutations resulted in insignificant changes in the PS capabilities (Fig. 3c, e, g). In addition, PhaSeMotif predicted important motifs of MLLT1 (Mut2/3) that are missed by other methods, which were verified to be essential for MLLT1 PS (Fig. 3h). Taken together, these results indicate that PhaSeMotif captures more precise motifs compared to existing methods.

Analysis of IDR motifs composition features revealed diverse clusters
After predicting motifs within high PS propensity IDRs, decoding the sequence features would advance our understanding of underlying principles. We constructed the IDR motifs dataset consisting of 17,594 predicted IDR motifs derived from 2418 IDRs (Supplementary Data 2, Methods). Both IDRs and motifs displayed high portion of disordered prompting residues such as proline, glutamic acid, serine and lysine (Fig. 4a)41. Furthermore, proline, serine and glycine were more significantly enriched in motifs, consistent with the previous finding that self-assembling PS proteins contain a higher portion of these residues11.

We next sought to cluster motifs based on sequence compositional features. The ratio of individual or two consecutive amino acids and each amino acid alphabet were calculated as basic sequence features (Supplementary Table 2). We also defined ‘abundant’ and ‘poly’ features which describe whether a particular amino acid is highly enriched and whether it appears consecutively multiple times. The distribution of each feature was then compared between high PS propensity IDRs, background IDRs, and IDR motifs, resulting in 207 significant sequence features (Supplementary Table 2, Supplementary Data 5). Considering the possible redundancy and linear/nonlinear relations between features, we applied autoencoder to perform dimensionality reduction. UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection)42 and DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise)43 were utilized to visualize and cluster the motifs (Fig. 4b, Methods). Consequently, nine clusters with diverse representative sequence features were identified. We clustered the motif using the sequence features and named them after the most representative residue types, namely Cluster 0, Polar, Positive, negative (Pos&Neg), Proline, Glycine, Positive, Aliphatic, Negative and Glutamine (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Fig. 4a).

To further dissect compositional features, we analyzed the relative amino acid abundance across motif clusters to further dissect their compositional features (Fig. 4d). The result is consistent with previous findings that different types of interactions between IDRs drive PS, including pi-pi, pi-cation, electrostatic, hydrophobic interactions and so on (Fig. 4d, Supplementary Fig. 4a)10. For example, aromatic residues (tyrosine and phenylalanine), along with glycine are relatively enriched in Cluster 0 and Cluster Glycine. Aromatic residues are important to mediate the pi-pi and pi-cation multivalent interactions driving the PS of Prion-like domain (PLD) containing proteins8,20. Cluster Pos&Neg, Positive and Negative motifs possess basic and/or acid amino acids, contributing to electrostatic interactions. In addition, the negatively and positive charged residues are separately distributed in Pos&Neg motifs, which are important for selective partitioning into condensates3,22,44. In addition, the abundance of proline and glycine in Cluster Proline and Glycine motif clusters may modulate IDRs disordered state, as these residues were highly enriched in PLDs and low complexity domains (LCDs)8. The result is consistent with a previous report that proline and glycine are enriched in putatively important residues in PS proteins15. Glutamine motif cluster encompassed repeated glutamine residues. Polyglutamine was found to mediated condensation through abundant hydrogen bonding and lead protein aggregation45, examples are HTT protein and Ataxin46,47. Among the clusters, Cluster 0 and Polar motifs are the most common, indicating they may act as fundamental units in PS IDRs. More than 90% of IDRs contain at least two types of motifs (Supplementary Fig. 4b). The Cluster 0 and Polar motifs are usually partnered with other types of motifs. IDRs containing both Cluster 0 motifs and other motifs displayed higher PhaSeMotif scores, suggesting their collaborative functions in promoting PS (Supplementary Fig. 4c). IDRs with only Cluster Glycine, Glutamine motifs are also presented with higher PhaSeMotif scores, consistent with their strong self-assembling capability. Interestingly, Pos&Neg, Positive and Negative motifs are usually presented together in IDRs, suggesting that opposite charged residues within one IDRs but located separately are important to electrostatic interactions (Supplementary Fig. 4c). Also, motifs with enriched charged residues frequently partner with cluster 0 and Polar motifs.

As motifs’ properties are related to interaction forces and thus condensates partitioning, we also looked into the motifs preference of proteins within known biomolecular condensates components extracted from PhaSepDB48,49. Most condensates were enriched in the most common Cluster 0 and Polar motifs (Fig. 4e). Proteins with Glycine motifs are enriched in paraspeckles, while proteins with Positive motifs are enriched in nuclear speckles and spliceosomes. (Fig. 4e). This is consistent with their functions closely associated with nucleic acids, interactions with which would involve charged motifs. There is emerging evidence that PS is involved in various molecular functions; we conducted functional enrichment of proteins with different motifs. Not surprisingly, non-membrane bounded organelles assembly is enriched in Cluster 0, Polar and charged motifs (Pos&Neg, Positive, and Negative), suggesting their essential roles in condensate formation (Fig. 4f). RNA-related functions are associated with Cluster 0, charged, and Glycine motifs (Fig. 4f). For example, previous studies have shown that the IDR of FMR1 is essential for its condensation with RNA, which regulates the translation process50. Together, these results indicate that PhaSeMotif identified IDR motifs whose combination provides hints for understanding the underlying molecular determinants of PS. In addition, the preferences of motifs for different condensates suggested that alteration in motifs might represent a possible way to modulate partitioning.

Generated motifs substitution validated the importance of compositional features
Thus far, we decoded the sequence features underlying IDR motifs and revealed diverse clusters. Theoretically, if the PS of motif-mutated IDRs can be restored via substituting motifs with similar features, the importance of underlying principles is validated. Hence, we built generative models to generate artificial motifs with features similar to the original ones but not identical in sequence. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are commonly used stable generative models51. Specifically, the motifs within each cluster were first encoded, sampled, and then decoded by re-integrating multiple convolution channels to learn the features of each category (Fig. 5a). We specifically focused on designing generative models to reflect the prominent sequence compositional features within the same clusters. This focused approach would allow us to reveal fundamental principles for PS motifs independent of specific IDRs. We developed a total of 9 VAE models corresponding to the 9 motif clusters. We used the trained autoencoder to project both the original and the generated motifs into the same latent space. The result indicates that the generated sequences are inherently similar to corresponding original clusters, the generated sequences are proximal to their corresponding original motifs (Supplementary Fig. 5a).

The accuracy of the generative models was further assessed by testing whether the generated sequences could be correctly re-clustered into the original one. The median re-clustering accuracy was above 0.85, suggesting the motif features were well captured by VAEs (Fig. 5b). Moreover, except for motifs with strong amino acid preferences such as Proline and Glycine motifs, the generated sequences are diverse in sequence and the median Needleman-Wunsch sequence similarity score was lower than 0.5 (Fig. 5b). This demonstrated that the models balanced both accuracy and diversity. To verify whether generated artificial motifs can substitute the original one, we first compared the overall PhaSeMotif prediction scores. For each PS IDR, we randomly selected 50 generated motifs of similar length within the same cluster, which were then used for ΔPhaSeMotif score calculation. The results showed the motif substitution led to subtle changes in most cases (Fig. 5b), suggesting that the generated sequences are computationally close to the native ones.

Next, the rescue experiments with a total of 21 generated artificial motifs covering 6 clusters were conducted (Table 1, Supplementary Data 4). Specifically, the (GGS)n linker in mutated IDRs aforementioned were replaced with generated motif sequences. For each motif cluster, we conducted rescue experiments for at least 2 generated sequences. In cluster 0, the generated sequences for TDP43 Mut2 and TIA1 Mut restore the PS capabilities (Fig. 5c). Similarly, the PS capabilities were generally restored for motifs in cluster Polar (Fig. 5d), Glycine (Fig. 5e), Pos&Neg (Fig. 5f), Proline (Fig. 5g) and Glutamine (Fig. 5h) compared to IDRs with mutated motifs, except for two motifs in cluster Proline and one motif in cluster Polar (Supplementary Fig. 5b-c). Notably, the PS capabilities of IDRs with generated motifs were comparable to those of wild-type IDRs for most sequences. Overall, 86% (18/21) generated motifs by PhaSeMotif were able to rescue the PS propensities caused by motif mutations, which strongly demonstrates the reliability of the generative models.

However, the varying degrees of restoration across different IDRs are observed. For instance, the generated motifs for TDP43 Mut showed stronger PS capabilities than WT (Fig. 5c). For TIA1, while the generated motifs ultimately displayed a similar number of condensates, its formation rate was slower than that of the WT (Fig. 5c). Additionally, the number of condensates for hnRNPH1 generated motifs and one of two generated motifs of MLLT1 Mut2 was smaller than that of WT (Fig. 5d). The generated motifs for TAF15 IDR1 Mut can restore the PS when tyrosine residues are added manually (Supplementary Fig. 5b). These results indicate that despite occasional non-identical PS restoration, our generative models can effectively capture the major principles of PS motifs. Overall, these results in mutations, generation and substitution of motifs demonstrated the feasibility of our proposed framework in investigating PS IDRs. With the help of predicting and generative models provided by PhaSeMotif, the underlying principles can be efficiently decoded.

## Methods

Construction of PhaSeMotif
A comprehensive summary of the machine learning dataset preparation, model construction, optimization, and evaluation, following the checklist recommended by Walsh et al.58., is provided in Supplementary Data 7.

Data preprocessing. To represent the input sequence, we employed a dual-channel encoding strategy for each amino acid. We first grouped the standard amino acids into a reduced alphabet of 9 classes based on their physicochemical side-chain properties (Supplementary Table 1). Each amino acid in the sequence was then converted into a 30-dimensional feature vector by concatenating two one-hot vectors: a 21-dimensional vector representing the specific amino acid type and a 9-dimensional vector representing its corresponding class in the reduced alphabet. The dual representation provides the model with both the specific residue identity and its general biochemical context.

Model architecture. The one-hot embeddings were passed to multiple two-dimensional convolution kernels with size of (21, 15) and (9, 15). The step size and padding were set as 1 and (0, 1). The two resulting feature maps were added and then transposed, with shape of (1, len, 8). A total of 8 multi-headed attention layers were set up to fully capture the local and global relationship between regions. The attention was calculated as

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V (1)

Here, Q is the query vector matrix. K is the key vector matrix and d_k is the dimension of the key vector. V is the value vector matrix. We set the shape of matrix of each head transformed from the input to V as (8, 1) to ensure that the resulted value obtained by each head is one-dimensional.

Spatial pyramid pooling. The length of the input amino acid sequence is arbitrary, so we generate a fixed-length feature vector through the pyramid pooling layer28. The length of the pooled data is determined by the division scale of the pyramid pooling layer. We set the division scale of the pyramid pooling layer to (1, 12) and allow overlaps between sub-regions.

Convolution and fully connected layers. We used a convolutional layer with 16 kernels with a shape of (5, 5) to further integrate the features. The stride and padding were 1. The feature map was transformed into a one-dimensional fully connected layer, which outputted the final probability.

Activation function, regularization, and model training. The ReLU activation function was adopted in each layer of the model. To prevent overfitting during training, we implemented a combination of regularization techniques, including dropout (p = 0.2), L2 regularization (λ = 0.001), batch normalization, and early stopping. The batch size of the model was 512. The training process adopted the cross-entropy loss function and the Adam optimization algorithm. By setting the pos_weight parameter to 3.5, the loss function would put more emphasis on correctly predicting the positive class, thus effectively mitigating the imbalance of the two classes during the training process. The step size of the Adam optimizer is set to 0.003. The model was developed using the Pytorch framework.

Model performance assessment
We use the ROC curve, the PR curve, and their corresponding AUC values to describe the model results and evaluate the performance of the classification model. The recall and precision were calculated as follows:

TPR (Recall) = TP / (TP + FN) (2)

FPR = FP / (FP + TN) (3)

where TP is True Positive, FN is False Negative, FP is False Positive, and TN is True Negative.

Model interpretation
First, the GBP algorithm was used to reveal the important regions that have a positive impact on prediction after the attention mechanism reorganizes the information. The GBP filtered out the regions with negative gradients that do not contribute or contribute little to the activation (Figs. 1B, 2A). We then selected the top 20 original regions with the highest attention scores as the positive sets for each positive region with positive forward and backward gradients. We defined the attribution score of each input region as the frequency of being included in the set. The top n regions with highest attribution scores were assigned as motifs. The cut off n can be calculated as 1 + int(length/30), which was designed to be related to the length of IDR. Overlapping regions were merged to final determined motifs.

Composition features screening
We defined sequence features for clustering, namely the basic single amino acid proportion, double amino acid proportion, alphabet proportion, abundant, and poly. When the proportion a type of amino acid in a 15-residue window exceeds 0.5, it was considered as “abundant”. When a type of amino acid appears continuously more than 6 times, it is considered “poly” and the number of times is calculated. (Supplementary Table 2). Next, the features in IDRs and motifs were compared and were retained the ones that were either significant between PS and non-PS IDRs or between motifs and PS IDRs. A total of 207 features were used for clustering (Supplementary Data 3). The statistical examination was from python scipy (v1.10.1).

Dimensionality reduction and clustering
First, we used autoencoder for dimensionality reduction to integrate linear and nonlinear relationships. The encoder and decoder were composed of fully connected layers with the ReLU activation function and 20-dimensional latent space. Next, UMAP was used for visualization (umap-learn v0.5.5). DBSCAN was used for preliminary clustering (scikit-learn v1.3.1). To evaluate the clustering results, we performed an independent t-test to reveal the significant features of each cluster. The clusters with fewer than 10 IDRs were removed and some clusters with similar features were grouped together.

Generative models and artificial sequences assessment
We adopted VAE as a generative framework. Specifically, we encoded the input sequence through convolution layers to generate multiple channels, then sampled in the latent space, and finally fuse the multiple channels back through a decoder to generate a new sequence. Considering the differences between clusters, we train a VAE model for each cluster respectively. The identified motifs were re-segmented into 15-residue sequences. The input one-hot encoding was the same as described above. The generated result is a matrix with a shape of (15, 21) and maximum normalized to be converted as one-hot embeddings, which can be translated into sequences. The resulting sequences were merged based on at least 3 head or tail amino acids to get sequences of various lengths.

The generated sequences were measured from two aspects: accuracy and diversity. Accuracy means whether the sequences can be correctly re-clustered using the same clustering parameters. Diversity means Needleman-Wunsch similarity between sequences within each cluster. The Needleman-Wunsch algorithm used was from the global mode of the PairwiseAligner in the Biopython (v1.81).

Extraction of important regions using alternative methods
We obtained the catGRANULES scores for each amino acid in the sequence through the catGRANULES web server [http://s.tartaglialab.com/new_submission/catGRANULES]. Regions with scores greater than 0 were considered significant. Due to the sliding window limitations of the catGRANULES method, the first 25 and last 25 amino acids in the sequence were not scored. Using the PLACC web server [http://plaac.wi.mit.edu/] with the default Core Length and the Homo sapiens background, we acquired scores where regions with values greater than 0.5 were deemed significant. We obtained scores using the PsPhunter web server [http://psphunter.stemcellding.org/index.php]. PsPhunter scores sites on a scale from 0 to 1, with smaller values indicating more significant regions; however, no explicit cutoff is defined. Due to the sliding window limitations of the method, the first 15 and last 15 amino acids in the sequence were not scored. The FuzDrop web server [https://fuzdrop.bio.unipd.it/predictor] directly provides the Droplet-promoting regions.

Cell culture
HeLa cells (ATCC CCL-2) were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (HyClone, Inc.) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Invitrogen, Inc.) at 37 °C with 5% CO2.

Plasmid construction and transfection
The pcDNA3.1-IDRs-mCherry-Cry2 plasmids encoding WT IDRs were provided by Dr. Pilong Li’s Lab and Dr. Xin Zhang’s Lab38,39. The DNA fragments encoding IDR mutants and IDR-generated sequences were synthesized (Supplementary Data 4) (GENEWIZ, INC SUZHOU) and cloned into pcDNA3.1-mCherry-Cry2 plasmid, respectively. HeLa cells were plated on 35 mm glass-bottom dishes (MatTek) and were transiently transfected with 1 μg of the plasmid. Transfections were performed using Lipofectamine 3000 (Thermo Fisher) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Then the cells were subjected to imaging and analysis 24- or 48-hours following transfection.

Live cell imaging and image analysis
All live cell imaging was performed using 60X oil immersion objective (NA 1.4) on a Nikon A1 laser scanning confocal microscope. Cells were imaged by use of laser wavelengths 488 nm for Cry2 activation and 561 nm for mCherry imaging. The duration of blue light stimulation varied from 1 to 12 seconds, while the imaging duration lasted between 1 to 3 minutes. Localized activation experiments were performed using the stimulation setting where the blue laser scans only a designated region of interest. Cells in one group are at similar expression levels and activated under identical conditions.

We employed CellProfiler version 4.2.6 to analyze the fluorescent images. The pipeline consisted of several steps: First, we converted raw RGB images to grayscale using the ColorToGray module. Next, we identified primary objects with a minimum diameter of 150 pixels using a global threshold strategy with the Minimum Cross-Entropy method. Then, we used the MaskObjects module to mask the identified primary objects and output them as ‘Cell’. Subsequently, we enhanced the speckle features of size 15 using the EnhanceOrSuppressFeatures module. We identified droplets as primary objects from the enhanced image with diameters between 3 to 40 pixels, employing an adaptive threshold strategy with the Robust Background method and a lower threshold of 0.2. Finally, we used the RelateObjects module to relate droplets (child) to cells (parent). Other parameters were set to their default values. For each sample, puncta were quantified in at least 10 cells (n ≥ 10).

### Reviewer 2

The authors provide a conceptually interesting approach to the challenge of predicting phase separation from sequence. The paper is well written and the approach not unreasonable, but there are unfortunately some major issues.
On the positive side of things, the paper is well written, the DL architecture is reasonable, and the authors have taken, I think, a conceptually reasonable approach to training /test /validation. Further, the authors have done a good job of experimentally testing predictions, although they make it extremely difficult to determine exactly what has been done (discussed below).
That said, I appreciate their conceptual approach here, in terms of using (GGS)n replacement (instead of just deletion) and NC controls based on regions that other predictors predict to be important (instead of cherry-picking obviously unimportant regions).
However, I do have some major concerns.
At a high level, I have philosophical concerns regarding whether deep learning predictors for “phase separation” are sensible. Absent any constraints on concentration, binding partners, or solution conditions, the question of ‘will my protein phase separate’ is simply “yes”. There will, of course, be solution conditions in which any polypeptide can be coaxed into forming two existing phases, perhaps far from physiological relevance but nevertheless possible. Therefore, the approach the authors are using here implicitly is not “a predictor of phase separation” but “a predictor of phase separation under physiological conditions”. Do the training/test/validation data support such a model?
The authors use predictions based on PhaSePred, which is trained on heterogeneous data from various sources, crucially, with no constraints on the underlying conditions. A protein may be annotated as “phase separating” even if this requires impossibly high concentrations of PEG. Similarly, the negative dataset used in PhaSePred does not include proteins that are not known to phase separate, but rather all other proteins from a set of proteomes that are distinct (as defined by similarity through CD-HIT) from those that have been “shown” to phase separate. From an epistemological standpoint, the assumption that “things that have not been reported in the literature to phase separate are non-phase separating” is a challenging position to support or defend.
As such, we’re left with two problems:
1. The authors presume it is reasonable to divide proteins into two classes: those that phase separate and those that do not. I find this worldview particularly hard to subscribe to, given that we know all proteins that phase separate do so under certain conditions, yet not under others, which immediately renders such a classification invalid.
2. Second, having made peace with that first assumption, we presume PhaSePred is able to distinguish between these two classes. Again, I am fundamentally unconvinced that methodologically, the approach used there makes any sense.
These two issues undermine the applicability of the work presented here. Now, these rather foundational issues notwithstanding, the work presented here is very good. But my major concern is that it’s built on a set of premises that do not make sense. If this is the case, we might expect evidence that the methodology has limited predictive power. Unfortunately, such evidence does emerge when testing the approach on sequences examined in this manuscript and beyond.
For example, the authors use the (GGS)n sequence to replace the motifs identified and find those sequences show reduced phase separation (Fig. 3). However, if you take the sequences (based on the information in the supplementary tables) and reconstruct a GGS-replaced version of the IDR used in the correlet system, all those GGS-containing sequences are strongly predicted to phase separate (despite the fact experimentally they do not). As such, my enthusiasm is somewhat dampened by the fact that it is not entirely clear whether the approach has really learned the residues that underlie phase separation, vs. those residues that co-occur with residues that drive phase separation.
For context, extensive work from many groups (Mittal, Banerjee, Mittal, Pappu, Hyman, Alberti, Forman-Kay etc.) has clearly shown how certain residues have an outside contribution to phase separation, yet in all studies to date glycine, proline, and serine have consistently shown up as “spacer” residues, those that are co-incident with residues that drive attractive intermolecular interactions but lack the requisite chemistry to drive attractive interactions to mediate phase separation. These spacer residues are typically far more abundant and provide a flexible but relatively inert scaffold within which other residues can sit. However, the compositional analysis in Fig. 4 suggests that the authors imply these residues underlie phase separation, when in fact the residues that have been demonstrably shown to drive phase separation (notably aromatic residues and arginine) are actually depleted from the motifs compared to general IDRs. Further, taking examples of sequences characterized previously (e.g., FUS LDC vs FUS Y2S variant) and generating a predicted score yields identical values, despite the fact that FUS Y2S is effectively infinitely soluble (no phase separation). Similar conclusions are arrived if we test other sequences where specific mutations have been made to suppress or enhance phase separation.
In short, my concerns here are essentially three-fold:
1. Do binary predictors of phase separation make sense? I think is a question the authors need to discuss extensively in a revised version.
2. Does the underlying approach for delineating phase separation vs. non-phase-separating proteins via PhaSePred work? The PhaSePred suffers from the same issues described in this review, so I think to convince readers of this the authors need to take as many examples of sequences where we have wildtype vs. variant data (of which there are many in the literature) where variant either enhances or suppresses phase separation, and ask if PhaSePred can correctly delineate between these two.
3. Does PhaSeMotif actually identify relevant subregions in proteins where specific mutations have been made to suppress or enhance phase separation?

2. However, I do have some major concerns.
At a high level, I have philosophical concerns regarding whether deep learning predictors for “phase separation” are sensible. Absent any constraints on concentration, binding partners, or solution conditions, the question of ‘will my protein phase separate’ is simply “yes”. There will, of course, be solution conditions in which any polypeptide can be coaxed into forming two existing phases, perhaps far from physiological relevance but nevertheless possible. Therefore, the approach the authors are using here implicitly is not “a predictor of phase separation” but “a predictor of phase separation under physiological conditions”. Do the training/test/validation data support such a model? The authors use predictions based on PhaSePred, which is trained on heterogeneous data from various sources, crucially, with no constraints on the underlying conditions. A protein may be annotated as “phase separating” even if this requires impossibly high concentrations of PEG. Similarly, the negative dataset used in PhaSePred does not include proteins that are not known to phase separate, but rather all other proteins from a set of proteomes that are distinct (as defined by similarity through CD-HIT) from those that have been “shown” to phase separate. From an epistemological standpoint, the assumption that “things that have not been reported in the literature to phase separate are non-phase separating” is a challenging position to support or defend. As such, we’re left with two problems:
1. The authors presume it is reasonable to divide proteins into two classes: those that phase separate and those that do not. I find this worldview particularly hard to subscribe to, given that we know all proteins that phase separate do so under certain conditions, yet not under others, which immediately renders such a classification invalid.
2. Second, having made peace with that first assumption, we presume PhaSePred is able to distinguish between these two classes. Again, I am fundamentally unconvinced that methodologically, the approach used there makes any sense.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful and fundamental critique, which provides us with an opportunity to clarify the conceptual framework and practical purpose of our work. Our study frames the PS prediction as an effort to distinguish between two protein populations with differential propensity for phase separation, rather than a definitive, binary classification of proteins into phase-separating and non-phase-separating classes.
1) The model is designed to predict propensity for phase separation rather than an absolute binary state. We fully agree with the reviewer that phase separation is a condition-dependent process, making a definitive binary classification scientifically challenging. Our work, as well as phase separation prediction tools such as PhaSePred (R6, 7), does not operate under the assumption that proteins exist in two immutable classes. Instead, we employed a binary classification as a principled computational abstraction to model a protein’s intrinsic, sequence-based propensity to phase separate.
2) The dataset construction is aligned with the goal of modeling differential phase separation propensity. The positive set is composed of proteins shown to phase separate either in cells or in vitro at moderate (often micromolar or lower) concentrations, providing a reasonable basis for a “high propensity” class. In contrast, by sampling from broader proteome, the negative set serves as a “background propensity” baseline, against which the enriched signals of the “high propensity” population can be identified through computational model training.
The significant difference in propensity makes the model robust to the inclusion of some yet-undiscovered phase-separating proteins. The usefulness of such strategy to sample negative set from background population has been examined in other phase separation predicting methods (R7–11) and in other areas such as protein-protein interaction prediction (R12), where the validated negative datasets are not readily available.
Given the framework, the utility of PhaSeMotif is to leverage the propensity differences to pinpoint the specific key regions within IDRs that are potentially to be functionally important for phase separation. The accuracy of our approach is supported by extensive mutagenesis experiments: mutations of 87% (20/23) predicted motifs markedly reduced or abolished PS.

This also explains the discrepancy the reviewer noted. When a functional motif is replaced in silico with a (GGS) linker, the model still captures an enrichment in glycine and serine. To investigate this further, we conducted the same in-silico substitution test on a range of widely used sequence-based predictors (Figure R1). This consistency supports the hypothesis that this issue is rooted in the inherent biases of current PS training datasets.
